*Opinionated piece, same caveat as the single cell design doc. These are my
views, not anyone's employer's.*

## Spatial is single cell with coordinates attached

That sentence is either a useful simplification or a trap, depending on which
part of the stack you are looking at.

For storage it is exactly right. A Visium spot is a barcode with counts against
it. The `SingleCells` class already keeps counts on disk in Rust binaries with
the metadata in a DuckDB, streams them in as needed, and scales to millions of
barcodes. Rebuilding all of that for spatial data would be daft. So
`SpatialSpot` inherits from `SingleCells` and gets the whole on-disk machinery
for free, plus HVG, PCA, neighbours and clustering, which all work on spots
without modification.

For the statistics it is wrong. Every spatial method in this package needs to
know which spots sit next to which other spots, and that information does not
live in the count matrix. It lives in the capture geometry. So the spatial layer
adds exactly two things: per-sample geometry and per-sample results keyed by
what produced them.

## The class

```r
SpatialSpot          # extends SingleCells
  samples            # named list of SpatialSample, keyed by exp_id
  sp_cache           # SpCache, per-sample results
```

A `SpatialSample` is a small S3 record: the technology, the spot count, the
scale factors out of `scalefactors_json.json`, which obs columns hold the
coordinates, and the relative paths of any registered slide images. One per
capture area. It carries no counts and no coordinates, only the metadata needed
to interpret them.

The coordinates themselves stay in the obs table, as `pxl_row_in_fullres` and
`pxl_col_in_fullres`. That is deliberate. They are per-spot metadata like any
other column, they survive filtering by the same mechanism, and a user who wants
to plot them can pull them with `get_sc_obs()` without learning a new accessor.
`get_spatial_coords()` exists as a convenience that returns them as a two-column
`(x, y)` matrix in graph order.

The `SpCache` holds six slots, all keyed by `exp_id` first:

```
per_sample_spatial_graph      exp_id -> dgCMatrix
per_sample_pca                exp_id -> list
per_sample_morans_i           exp_id -> SpMoransRes
per_sample_sparkx             exp_id -> SpSparkxRes
per_sample_nhood_enrichment   exp_id -> label_col -> SpNhoodRes
per_sample_image_features     exp_id -> resolution -> SpImageFeatures
```

The last two nest a second level because the result is not a property of the
sample alone. Neighbourhood enrichment against cluster labels and against
pathologist annotations are two different answers about the same slide, and both
are worth keeping. Same for image features cut from `hires` and from
`cytassist`.

### Why per sample and not global

Two capture areas have two coordinate systems. Spot 1 of sample A and spot 1 of
sample B are unrelated points, and a graph built over the union of their
coordinates would happily connect them if the pixel ranges overlap, which they
usually do. Nothing about that failure is loud. You get a graph, the statistics
run, and the numbers are nonsense.

So the graph is per sample, the statistics loop over samples, and there is no
global spatial anything.

### Results are data.tables wearing a hat

`SpMoransRes` and `SpSparkxRes` are `data.table`s with an extra class in front.
That is on purpose: users want a `data.table`, and the class only buys a `print`
method that does not dump 19,000 rows and a diagnostic `plot`.

The cost is that `[.data.table` and `merge()` carry the class onto anything
derived from the result. Merge a Moran's I table with a SPARK-X one, summarise
it to a single row, and the summary is still an `SpMoransRes` as far as dispatch
is concerned, without any of the columns the print method wants. The print
methods fall back to printing the plain table when the columns are missing, so
this is cosmetic rather than fatal, but the tidiest habit is to pull the columns
you want into a fresh `data.table` before you start deriving from them.

### The S3-on-S7 trap

The `SpCache` getters and setters are S3 generics. `class()` of an S7 object is
`c("bixverse::SpatialSpot", "bixverse::SingleCells", "S7_object")`, so a method
named `get_per_sample_spatial_graph.SpatialSpot` never dispatches. It is not an
error. R finds no method, falls through to the default, and you get `NULL`
forever.

This has bitten three separate times in this codebase. The methods have to be
registered through `S7::method()`, and there is a test asserting that the getter
comes back `NULL` before the graph is built and non-`NULL` after, which is the
only cheap way to catch a generic that silently does nothing.

## Index spaces

Five index spaces cross the R/Rust boundary here, and they are not the same.

| thing                        | base | space                                |
|------------------------------|------|--------------------------------------|
| DuckDB `cell_idx`            | 1    | global                               |
| `get_spot_indices_for_exp()` | 0    | global                               |
| `spots_to_keep` into Rust    | 0    | global                               |
| neighbour / weight lists     | 0    | local, positional vs `spots_to_keep` |
| labels into the permutation  | 0    | local                                |
| coordinates                  | n/a  | full-res pixels, `(x, y)`            |

The one worth internalising: the neighbour lists are **local**. Entry `i`
describes the spot at row `i` of the coordinate matrix, and the indices inside
it position against that same matrix. They are not global spot ids. That is what
makes `MoransI::new()`'s check `neighbours.len() == spots_to_keep.len()` a real
check rather than a coincidence.

Coordinates are always in full-resolution pixels, never pre-scaled. The image
scale factor is applied inside Rust. Pre-scaling on the R side and then handing
over a scale factor as well is the obvious way to get tiles at the wrong place,
and it produces plausible-looking features rather than an error.

## The spatial graph

Four layouts. Two of them are exact.

`hex` and `square` are table look-ups over the array coordinates and never
compute a distance. On the Visium honeycomb `array_col` steps by two inside a
row and odd rows are offset by one, so the six neighbours of `(r, c)` are
`(r, c ± 2)` and `(r ± 1, c ± 1)`. A corollary is that
`array_row % 2 == array_col % 2` holds for every spot, which is why the offsets
never leave the lattice. Getting the parity wrong drops an interior spot to four
neighbours and nothing complains.

A kNN with `k = 6` on the same lattice gets close but not identical, because the
pixel pitch is anisotropic: in-row neighbours sit 100 px apart on the fixture
geometry and out-of-row ones 100.34 px. Close enough that a kNN mostly works and
occasionally does not. If the capture geometry is known, use it.

`knn` and `radius` are there for Xenium and MERFISH, where there is no lattice
to exploit.

### W versus W + Wᵀ

The `SpCache` stores the graph as the raw directed adjacency, exactly as the
builder returned it. Every statistic symmetrises internally: reciprocal entries
`(i, j)` and `(j, i)` get folded into `w_ij + w_ji` and scattered back into both
rows, so what the statistics actually see is always `W + Wᵀ`.

This matters for one number. `rs_sp_build_graph()` returns
`list(indices, weights, degree)`, and **`degree` is the row sum of the
symmetrised graph, not the neighbour count**. On a reciprocal binary lattice it
is exactly twice the neighbour count: median 6 neighbours, median degree 12. Use
`lengths(indices)` if you want a count of neighbours. The two are not the same
number and only one of them is called something that sounds like it.

Row normalisation makes this worse, in the sense of more confusing: with
`row_normalise = TRUE` every row sums to one, so the degree is 2 everywhere and
carries no information at all.

Moran's I is invariant to a uniform scaling of `W`, so doubling the whole matrix
changes nothing about `I`, `E[I]` or `Var[I]`. That is what makes the
symmetrisation free rather than a decision.

## Moran's I

```
I = (N / S0) * sum_ij w_ij (x_i - mean)(x_j - mean) / sum_i (x_i - mean)^2
```

with the normality null, not the randomisation one:

```
E[I]   = -1 / (N - 1)
Var[I] = (N^2 S1 - N S2 + 3 S0^2) / (S0^2 (N^2 - 1)) - E[I]^2
```

This is the Cliff-Ord closed form, and it is chosen specifically so the answer
matches `spdep::moran.test(randomisation = FALSE)`. There is a test pinning it
against spdep on a synthetic lattice: `E[I]` and `Var[I]` agree to ten decimal
places and `I` to the limit of the `f32` the kernel runs in, about six
significant figures. A second pin takes the rank correlation against Space
Ranger's own `spatial_enrichment.csv` on a real slide, which comes out at 0.99.

`E[I]` and `Var[I]` are scalars across genes. They depend on `N` and on the
graph weights and on nothing else, so they get computed once and per-gene work
collapses to one sparse quadratic form plus a sum of squares. 18,945 genes over
3,827 spots takes about 200 ms.

### The normalisation trap

Moran's I runs on normalised counts by default, and that couples every gene to
every other gene through the library size. Plant one loud marker on half the
slide, big enough to shift the library size where it is expressed, and the
denominator drags spatial structure into genes that have none. The first
synthetic fixture written for this had a pure-noise gene scoring `I = 0.19`.

For real data this is the right default: you want autocorrelation of expression,
not of sequencing depth. For building a test fixture it is a trap, and
`params_sp_svg(assay = "raw")` is the way out.

### Constant genes

A gene with zero variance has no defined `I`. Rust emits `NaN` and the `Z` and
p-value follow. The BH step then maps those `NaN` p-values to an FDR of zero, so
constant genes come back looking significant and lead the top-gene table in the
`print` method. Filter on `is.finite(morans_i)` before you read the FDR column.
With the default gene QC (`min_cells = 10`) there are no constant genes and the
issue never shows up; drop `min_cells` to zero and roughly half the feature space
is constant.

## SPARK-X

Kernel-based, non-parametric, and it needs no graph at all: it works straight off
the coordinates. Ten kernels by default, five Gaussian and five cosine, with
bandwidths taken from quantiles of the pairwise distance distribution on a
sub-sample. Per-kernel p-values get Cauchy-combined.

It is much more liberal than Moran's I on the same data. On the example slide
Moran's I calls 11,980 genes at 5% FDR and SPARK-X calls 17,401, with 11,737 in
common. That is not a bug in either; they are testing different nulls. Moran's I
asks whether neighbouring spots agree, SPARK-X asks whether expression covaries
with position under any of ten smooth kernels, and almost everything expressed
does a bit of the latter.

Run both. Take the intersection when you want a short list.

## Neighbourhood enrichment

Permute the labels, keep the graph. The null then carries the spatial structure
of the slide, which is the whole point: a label that happens to sit on 40% of
the spots will co-occur with itself a lot under any null, and a null that
reshuffled the graph instead would not know that.

The output is a K x K Z-score matrix. On the example slide, Leiden clusters at
resolution 0.8 give a diagonal with a median Z of 61 and an off-diagonal median
of -8, which is what spatially coherent domains look like. The interesting
entries are the positive off-diagonal ones: those are compartments that touch.

## Images

The honest section.

### The resolution problem

Space Ranger ships a `hires` PNG, a `lowres` PNG and a CytAssist TIFF. On the
example slide a spot is 256 px across at full resolution, which becomes:

| resolution | scale factor | spot diameter |
|------------|--------------|---------------|
| `lowres`   | 0.0168       | 4.3 px        |
| `hires`    | 0.0561       | 14.4 px       |
| `cytassist`| 0.0842       | 21.6 px       |

First-order colour statistics on a 14 px tile are fine. Haralick texture off a
grey-level co-occurrence matrix on a 14 px tile is close to noise: you have
roughly 200 pixels, you are quantising them to 32 grey levels, and you are asking
for a second-order statistic. The numbers come back, they are finite, and they
mean very little.

Texture features do not become meaningful until a real scanner slide is
registered under `fullres`, and Space Ranger does not ship one. The example data
offers nothing above 21.6 px. So the texture block exists, it is correct, and on
the data most people have it is not worth reading.

### The formats

Generic tiled TIFF is the only container that has actually been through this
code. **No vendor slide format has ever been tested.** Not SVS, not NDPI, not
MIRAX. The backend probes the file rather than trusting its extension and hands
it to OpenSlide first, so in principle a vendor slide should work and the pyramid
table should come back populated. In practice nobody has run one through it, and
"in principle" is not a claim worth making about file formats.

The `spatial-image` feature also means OpenSlide is a hard build and run
dependency. That is a C library, it has to be present at compile time, and it is
new as a `SystemRequirements` entry for this package.

### The asymmetry that looks like a bug

```r
get_image(object, "example", "cytassist")
#> Error: ... is a TIFF. TIFFs can be registered but not yet loaded.

image_features_sp(object, resolution = "cytassist")
#> works fine
```

Both are true at once. The R side reads PNG and JPEG through `png` and `jpeg`
and has no TIFF reader. The Rust side reads TIFF perfectly well, because that is
what the image backend is for. So you can compute features off the CytAssist
frame but you cannot pull it into R to look at it.

This is not a deliberate design. It is where the two halves happened to land, and
it is worth knowing before you spend an afternoon on it.

## What is deliberately not here

**Per-sample PCA.** The `SpCache` has the slot and nothing fills it. Global PCA
across samples works today through the inherited `calculate_pca_sc()`, and that
is the right default for anything you then want to cluster jointly. Per-sample
PCA is for when you do not.

**Superspots.** `MetaSpot` exists and holds aggregated counts at metaspot
resolution, but there is no `generate_superspot_*` to produce one. Spatially
aware aggregation is a different problem from the kNN-based meta cell methods,
and doing it badly is worse than not doing it.

**Image-free ingest.** `load_visium()` wants a Space Ranger directory. If you
have counts and coordinates and no slide, there is currently no path in.

**h5ad.** Squidpy and scanpy write spatial data into `adata.obsm['spatial']` and
`adata.uns['spatial']`. Reading that is the obvious next thing and it is not
done.
